definition: Conflicted means torn between opposing feelings or loyalties.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word conflicted. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know conflicted should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Otis felt conflicted at the auction: bidding on the vintage press meant outbidding the museum where he had volunteered for years.
Uneasy is fainter than conflicted — a low hum of discomfort without two loyalties actually at war.
Anguished goes further than conflicted: the inner tug-of-war has broken into open pain.

Divided means split between sides — a committee, a family, or a single mind pulled toward opposing camps. Conflicted is more personal and more painful: the split runs between loyalties, so that serving either one feels like betraying the other. A vote can be divided; a heart is conflicted.

Split means cut cleanly into two camps or impulses — the sharpest, plainest version of being of two minds. Conflicted adds the ache: its two sides are loyalties or duties at war, so the person suffers the split rather than simply containing it.

Offered the anchor chair in another city, the reporter was openly conflicted — the job she had chased for a decade on one side, her mother's Sunday dinners and her hometown sources on the other.
Conflicted is stronger and more specific than 'unsure': it means two loyalties or desires are at war inside you, so that serving either one feels like betraying the other.
Conflicted is the word for loyalty pulled two ways — job against family, evidence against sympathy.
Where its unit-mate ambivalent reports mixed feelings, conflicted stages a fight between them; the stakes are duties, not just moods.

When the request arrived from the island nation, curator Ruth Odell read it twice and put it in a drawer for a week.
The carved canoe prow had anchored her museum's Pacific hall for thirty years; she had built her career explaining it to schoolchildren.
Her diary that month shows a woman deeply conflicted.
The museum had trained her, promoted her, trusted her with its collection — and the letter was right that the prow had left the island under terms no one would defend today.
'To keep it betrays people I have never met,' she wrote.
'To return it betrays the hall I have spent my life building.
There is no move that is loyal to both.' She recommended return in the spring, and wrote that the decision felt less like relief than like choosing which promise to break.
